judge_assessment.explanation: The ACCEPT and every arithmetic claim hold up under independent recomputation: 8+5=13, 12-5=7, 7+8=15, 9+7=16, 16-7=9, 13-4=9 for the missing-start subtraction, 6+8=14, 15-7=8, 5+7=12, and the fact family 4+9=13, 13-9=4, 13-4=9. One judge artifact_finding is factually wrong, however. The judge writes 'item 10 intentionally contains three related blanks'; worksheet.tex renders FOUR answer slots in problem 10 -- '$4 + \ $\ansblank$ \ = \ $\ansblank' is two blanks, then one each for '13 - 9 =' and '13 - 4 ='. verify.json carries three entries under id 10 and the missing addend (9) appears only as an input, at.b, of the a+b check rather than as a verified expected. The visible consequence is in the delivered key: the Quick Answers bank prints '10. 13, 4, 9' -- three values for four blanks, and in an order that does not match the reading order of the blanks, which is 9, 13, 4, 9. A parent checking problem 10 against the bank alone cannot line the numbers up with the slots.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 6 puts the blank in the FIRST position of a subtraction ('__ - 4 = 9'), the one placement where subtracting the two printed numbers fails, and the key names the exact wrong answer that slip produces: 'a child who writes 5 here has computed 9 - 4. Ask them to read the sentence aloud.' That pairing of a deliberately awkward placement with its diagnostic wrong answer is the strongest thing on the sheet.

Problem 5 (16 - 7) is the undoing of problem 4 (9 + 7) and is placed apart from it on purpose, with the key's step 1 saying so -- interleaving that actually forces method choice rather than alternating labels.
Every worked solution's Step 1 names WHICH KIND of problem it is before any arithmetic happens, which is exactly the decision the interleaved format is meant to teach.

root_causes.description: The coverage rule is per-problem-id, not per-printed-response. SKILL.md states that verification hard-fails unless every problem id 1..N has at least one check, so a problem that renders four \ansblank slots satisfies the contract with three entries -- or with one. Nothing in the gate chain compares the number of answer-location macros a problem prints against the number of expecteds bound to that id.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 10 renders four \ansblank macros; verify.json has three entries for id 10.
The missing addend 9 is never an 'expected' -- it appears only as at.b in {'expr': 'a + b', 'at': {'a': 4, 'b': 9}, 'expected': 13}.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '10. 13, 4, 9' against four printed slots whose reading order is 9, 13, 4, 9.
gate_log.txt records answer-line-ws PASS and a green build, so no gate noticed.

improvements.title: Bind verification to each printed answer slot rather than to the problem id
improvements.proposed_change: Change the coverage contract in SKILL.md from 'every problem id carries at least one check' to 'every rendered answer-location macro carries a check or an explicit manual entry'. tests/check_layout.py already parses answer-location macros per item; extend it to count \ansblank, \ansline and bare \underline{\hspace{...}} response rules inside each \problem body and fail the build when a problem renders more response rules than its verify entries supply expecteds for. For fact-family items like problem 10, that forces a fourth entry pinning the missing addend (a solve for 4 + x = 13), and it lets the Quick Answers bank print one value per slot in reading order.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture worksheet whose problem renders four \ansblank macros while its verify.json supplies three expecteds under that id. tests/check_layout.py must exit non-zero and name the uncovered slot. Against today's code the fixture passes (curr-040 built green with exactly that shape); after the fix it fails, and the sibling fixture with a fourth entry passes.
improvements.expected_impact: Every blank a student is asked to fill is either machine-checked or explicitly manual, and the Quick Answers bank stops printing fewer values than the worksheet has slots.
improvements.risk: Fixtures and existing verify.json files that under-count slots will start failing the gate, so a sweep of the authored corpus is needed alongside the change; the macro count must not mistake a decorative rule (the name/date header) for a response slot.

case_summary: A genuinely well-interleaved within-20 sheet whose mathematics is exact everywhere I checked it (12 machine checks plus 6 study-guide checks, all correct) and whose warm-up-then-interleave-then-synthesise structure does what the prompt asked. final_response.md names all three PDFs, so the surface-artifacts finding does not apply here, and with no compare entries the Quick Answers bank prints a real value on every row. The one defect is coverage granularity: problem 10 prints four blanks and verify.json covers three, with the missing addend surviving only as an input to another check, so the delivered Quick Answers row cannot be read slot-by-slot. The 32/32 is defensible; the judge's description of problem 10 as having three blanks is not.
